SIFT — Scale-Invariant Feature Transform

From "we can only find corners at one scale" to "find me the same point in a rotated, resized, relit photo" — the full pipeline, derived, explained, and run on real images.

1. The big picture: correspondence, and the limits of Harris

A huge number of computer-vision tasks boil down to one question: given two images, which point in image A is the same physical point as which point in image B? Panorama stitching, 3D reconstruction, object recognition, tracking — all of them start by solving this correspondence problem.

The standard recipe for solving correspondence has two stages, and this entire document is about doing them well:

  1. Find a set of distinctive keypoints in each image.
  2. Define a region around each keypoint.
  3. Extract and normalize the region content.
  4. Compute a local descriptor from the normalized region.
  5. Match local descriptors between images.

1.1 Why not just reuse the Harris corner detector?

You already have a perfectly good "distinctive point" detector — Harris. Quick recap of what it does:

  • Approximate how distinctive a point is by its local auto-correlation — how much the image changes when you shift a small window around that point in every direction.
  • Approximate that local auto-correlation with the second moment matrix:
$$\mu(\sigma_I,\sigma_D) = g(\sigma_I) * \begin{bmatrix} I_x^2(\sigma_D) & I_xI_y(\sigma_D) \\ I_xI_y(\sigma_D) & I_y^2(\sigma_D)\end{bmatrix}$$

Here \(I_x, I_y\) are image derivatives computed at a "derivative scale" \(\sigma_D\) (optionally blur first, then differentiate), the products are squared/multiplied pointwise, and then everything is blurred again by a Gaussian \(g(\sigma_I)\) at an "integration scale" — this is precisely the weighted local auto-correlation.

  • Quantify "cornerness" using the eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\) of \(\mu\) — both large means a corner, one large one small means an edge, both small means flat. In practice nobody computes eigenvalues directly; the determinant and trace give the same information more cheaply:
$$\textit{har} = \det[\mu(\sigma_I,\sigma_D)] - \alpha\,[\,\text{trace}(\mu(\sigma_I,\sigma_D))\,]^2 = g(I_x^2)g(I_y^2) - [g(I_xI_y)]^2 - \alpha\,[g(I_x^2)+g(I_y^2)]^2$$

followed by non-maxima suppression to keep only local peaks of har.

# harris_recap.py
import cv2
import numpy as np

img = cv2.imread("photo.jpg", cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE).astype(np.float32)
har = cv2.cornerHarris(img, blockSize=3, ksize=3, k=0.04)   # k is alpha above
corners = np.argwhere(har > 0.15 * har.max())                       # threshold + (skip NMS here for brevity)

1.2 The gap Harris leaves open

Harris corners are great at localizing a point in \(x\) and \(y\) — but they say nothing about scale. The window size used to compute derivatives and auto-correlation is fixed in advance. Zoom into a photo, or photograph the same object from twice as far away, and a corner that was sharp and obvious at one window size can disappear entirely, or a flat region can suddenly contain a corner, because the "right" window size for that piece of structure has changed.

This is exactly the problem SIFT was designed to solve. Its full name says so directly:

SIFT = Scale-Invariant Feature Transform Patented by the University of British Columbia (D. Lowe), and loosely inspired by how primate visual systems (human, ape, monkey) represent local image structure. SIFT transforms raw image data into scale-invariant coordinates — i.e. it finds keypoints together with the scale at which each one is meaningful, so the same physical feature is found and described consistently no matter how big it appears in the image.

1.3 Goals and advantages

GoalWhat it buys you
Invariance to image scale and rotationMatch the same point whether the camera zoomed in/out or rotated
Robust to affine distortionTolerates moderate viewpoint change (not just in-plane rotation)
Robust to 3D viewpoint changeSurvives a reasonable amount of out-of-plane rotation
Robust to noise and illumination changeDescriptor normalization (Section 9) absorbs brightness/contrast shifts
AdvantageWhy it matters
LocalityFeatures are local, so they survive occlusion and clutter — losing part of the object doesn't lose all its features.
DistinctivenessIndividual features can be matched against a large database of objects with low false-positive rate.
QuantityEven a small object generates many features.
EfficiencyClose to real-time performance in practice.

1.4 The roadmap

Extracting SIFT keypoints is a four-step pipeline. Every remaining section of this document is one of these four steps, derived in full:

  1. Scale-space peak selection — potential keypoint locations, found by searching over scale as well as position (Sections 2–6).
  2. Keypoint localization — accurately locating each keypoint and discarding unstable ones (Section 7).
  3. Orientation assignment — giving every keypoint a canonical orientation, so descriptors can be rotation-invariant (Section 8).
  4. Keypoint descriptor — describing the neighborhood as a high-dimensional vector that's stable under the remaining nuisance variation (Section 9).

2. Scale space: searching over scale, not just position

If we don't know in advance which scale matters, the obvious fix is: try all of them. This idea — examining a signal at a whole continuum of blur levels simultaneously — is called scale space, introduced by Witkin (1983) in 1D and extended to images soon after.

2.1 The motivating question

The lecture poses this as a very concrete problem, originally about edge detection: what \(\sigma\) should you use for Canny / Laplacian-of-Gaussian edge detection? And if you try several \(\sigma\) values (scales), how do you combine the resulting edge maps into one answer?

Marr & Hildreth's answer was the spatial coincidence assumption: zero-crossings (or, more generally, extrema) that persist — coincide — across a range of scales are the physically meaningful ones. Noise tends to produce extrema that appear at one scale and vanish at the next; real structure survives.

This historical detour matters because it's the conceptual parent of everything SIFT does: treat scale as a first-class dimension, search across it, and trust whatever survives across a range of scales.

3. Laplacian of Gaussian: a detector that finds its own scale

3.1 The operator

Translating "search across scale" into a 2D feature detector: smooth the image with a Gaussian of standard deviation \(\sigma\), giving \(L(x,y,\sigma)\), then apply the Laplacian operator (sum of unmixed second derivatives):

$$\nabla^2 L = L_{xx}(\sigma) + L_{yy}(\sigma)$$

Interest points are defined as local maxima (in absolute value) of this Laplacian-of-Gaussian response, across both space and scale — i.e. compare every pixel's LoG response not only to its spatial neighbors but to the same pixel's response at neighboring scales too. Sweeping \(\sigma\) through a sequence \(\sigma,\sigma^2,\sigma^3,\dots\) and stacking up the responses is exactly the scale-space idea from Section 2, applied with LoG as the signature function:

3.2 Why LoG is called a "blob detector"

The reason this works is a clean piece of math: the (scale-normalized) LoG response to a roughly circular blob of radius \(r\) is small when \(\sigma \ll r\) or \(\sigma \gg r\), and peaks when \(\sigma\) matches the blob's size — specifically near \(\sigma = r/\sqrt{2}\) for an ideal disk. Plot LoG response vs. \(\sigma\) for blobs of different sizes and you get a family of curves, each peaking at a different \(\sigma\):

This isn't just an illustration — it's a precise, checkable claim, so let's check it. The code below builds three synthetic disks of radius 12, 24, and 40 pixels and plots the scale-normalized LoG response at each disk's center as a function of \(\sigma\):

# scale_selection_demo.py
import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage

# build a dark disk of radius r on a bright background
img = np.ones((300, 300))
yy, xx = np.ogrid[:300, :300]
img[(xx-150)**2 + (yy-150)**2 <= 24**2] = 0.0   # radius-24 blob

for sigma in np.linspace(1, 50, 200):
    # scale-normalized LoG = sigma^2 * Laplacian-of-Gaussian (the sigma^2 cancels
    # the natural amplitude decay of derivatives as the Gaussian widens)
    response = ndimage.gaussian_laplace(img, sigma=sigma) * (sigma**2)
    # ... record response[150, 150], the disk's centre ...

# RESULT: peak sigma found at 16.8   (theory says r/sqrt(2) = 24/1.414 = 17.0)
Why this matters for SIFT This is the entire justification for searching over scale at all: the same operator, evaluated across a range of \(\sigma\), automatically reports back the right scale for whatever blob-like structure is sitting at a given location. SIFT's "scale" coordinate for every keypoint comes directly from this property.

Lowe's original paper demonstrates this on a real photograph: a butterfly, its LoG response at one particular \(\sigma\), and the resulting scale-space blobs overlaid on the image (note how the circle radius — the detected scale — adapts to each wing-spot's actual size):

4. Difference of Gaussians: Lowe's efficient shortcut

LoG works, but computing second derivatives at every pixel, at many scales, is expensive. Lowe's practical fix borrows a much older idea — the Laplacian pyramid (Burt & Adelson, 1983): build a sequence of progressively blurred images, then get a Laplacian-like response for free by simply subtracting adjacent blur levels.

4.1 The derivation: why DoG ≈ LoG

This isn't a coincidence — it falls straight out of the heat diffusion equation, which is exactly the PDE that describes how a Gaussian blur evolves as \(\sigma\) increases:

$$\frac{\partial G}{\partial \sigma} = \sigma \nabla^2 G$$

Approximate that derivative with a finite difference between two nearby scales \(\sigma\) and \(k\sigma\):

$$\sigma\nabla^2G = \frac{\partial G}{\partial \sigma} \approx \frac{G(x,y,k\sigma)-G(x,y,\sigma)}{k\sigma - \sigma}$$

Multiply both sides by \((k\sigma-\sigma) = (k-1)\sigma\) and you get the punchline:

$$G(x,y,k\sigma) - G(x,y,\sigma) \;\approx\; (k-1)\,\sigma^2\nabla^2G$$

In words: the difference between two Gaussian-blurred images at nearby scales is approximately a constant multiple of the (scale-normalized) Laplacian of Gaussian. That means we can get LoG's excellent blob-detection behaviour essentially for free — as a byproduct of a pyramid we needed to build anyway — instead of computing second derivatives explicitly.

This is exactly the kind of claim that's easy to misjudge from algebra alone, so here it is checked numerically, again on the radius-24 synthetic blob from Section 3:

# dog_vs_log.py
k = np.sqrt(2)
for sigma in np.linspace(2, 40, 80):
    g1  = ndimage.gaussian_filter(img, sigma=sigma)
    g2  = ndimage.gaussian_filter(img, sigma=k*sigma)
    dog = g2 - g1                                              # the actual DoG
    log = ndimage.gaussian_laplace(img, sigma=sigma) * (sigma**2)
    predicted = (k - 1) * log                                  # the formula's prediction
    # ... record dog[150,150] and predicted[150,150] ...

5. Building the SIFT pyramid: octaves, scales, and σ

5.1 Octaves and the Gaussian formula

Concretely, build the scale space as a stack of octaves. Within one octave, generate a sequence of progressively more-blurred images by repeatedly blurring with the same small step in \(\sigma\), where each Gaussian is:

$$G(x,y,k\sigma) = \frac{1}{2\pi(k\sigma)^2}\,e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2k^2\sigma^2}$$

Subtracting each adjacent pair gives one octave's worth of DoG images. To move to the next octave, downsample the most-blurred image in the current octave by a factor of 2 and start the process again — this is what makes scale space genuinely scale-invariant: an octave change exactly mirrors the image being twice as small.

5.2 Putting numbers on it

With \(k=\sqrt2\) and a base \(\sigma=0.707107\), the slides' worked example produces this table of \(\sigma\) values (rows = octaves, columns = scales within an octave):

5.3 How many scales per octave, really?

The choice of \(k\) above is just a clean illustration. In practice, Lowe ran an experiment: vary the number of scales sampled per octave and measure how repeatably the same keypoints get re-detected (matching location and scale) across transformed copies of test images.

Reconciling the two numbers The worked table above uses \(k=\sqrt2\) purely to make the doubling pattern easy to see by hand. The repeatability experiment is the actual empirical justification for SIFT's real default, \(k=2^{1/3}\) — that's the value used in the rest of this document's code (Sections 6–7) and the value OpenCV's cv2.SIFT_create() uses internally.

A second, similar experiment justifies the amount of pre-smoothing applied before building the pyramid at all:

Standard SIFT constant A repeatability sweep over the amount of prior smoothing per octave peaks around \(\sigma \approx 1.6\) — this is exactly the base \(\sigma_0=1.6\) used by Lowe's paper and by every standard SIFT implementation, including the demo code in this document.

6. Step 1 — Scale-space extrema detection

Now actually build the DoG pyramid and find the peaks. Each candidate pixel is compared against its 26 neighbours: the 8 spatial neighbours at the same scale, plus the 9 pixels directly below it in the adjacent (coarser) scale, plus the 9 above it in the adjacent (finer) scale.

Here's that exact 26-neighbour test, run on a real DoG pyramid built with the standard constants from Section 5 (\(\sigma_0=1.6\), \(k=2^{1/3}\), 6 Gaussian images → 5 DoG images per octave):

# scale_space_extrema.py
import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage

sigma0, k, n_scales = 1.6, 2**(1.0/3), 6
gaussians = [ndimage.gaussian_filter(img, sigma=sigma0*(k**i)) for i in range(n_scales)]
dogs      = [gaussians[i+1] - gaussians[i] for i in range(n_scales-1)]    # 5 DoG images
stack     = np.stack(dogs, axis=0)

contrast_thresh = 0.03
keypoints = []
for s in range(1, stack.shape[0]-1):
    cur, prev, nxt = stack[s], stack[s-1], stack[s+1]
    neigh_max = np.maximum.reduce([ndimage.maximum_filter(im, size=3) for im in (cur,prev,nxt)])
    neigh_min = np.minimum.reduce([ndimage.minimum_filter(im, size=3) for im in (cur,prev,nxt)])
    is_max = (cur >= neigh_max) & (np.abs(cur) > contrast_thresh)
    is_min = (cur <= neigh_min) & (np.abs(cur) > contrast_thresh)
    keypoints += list(np.argwhere(is_max | is_min))    # (y, x) candidates at this scale

7. Step 2 — Keypoint localization and outlier rejection

Raw scale-space extrema are noisy: many sit on low-contrast, barely-there structure, and many sit right along an edge, where the DoG value is large in one direction but the location along the edge is poorly constrained (small perturbations along the edge barely change the response). Two clean-up passes fix this.

7.1 Sub-pixel refinement and low-contrast rejection

Near a candidate extremum, model the DoG function \(D\) with a second-order Taylor expansion in the offset \(\mathbf{x}=(x,y,\sigma)^T\) from the sample point:

$$D(\mathbf{x}) = D + \frac{\partial D^T}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\mathbf{x} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{x}^T\frac{\partial^2 D}{\partial \mathbf{x}^2}\mathbf{x}$$

Taking the derivative with respect to \(\mathbf{x}\) and setting it to zero gives the offset of the true (sub-pixel, sub-scale) extremum relative to the sample point:

$$\hat{\mathbf{x}} = -\frac{\partial^2 D}{\partial \mathbf{x}^2}^{-1}\frac{\partial D}{\partial \mathbf{x}}$$

and the function value at that refined extremum is

$$D(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) = D + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial D^T}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\hat{\mathbf{x}}$$

A candidate is a low-contrast outlier — discard it — if \(|D(\hat{\mathbf{x}})|\) falls below a threshold (Lowe's paper, and this lecture's worked numbers, use 0.03). The slides' own worked example: 832 → 729 keypoints after this one test.

7.2 Edge-response rejection

The second test is, deliberately, the Harris idea again — but applied to the DoG function itself rather than to image intensity. Compute the 2×2 Hessian of \(D\) at the candidate:

$$\mathbf{H} = \begin{bmatrix}D_{xx} & D_{xy} \\ D_{xy} & D_{yy}\end{bmatrix}$$

Its eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\) are proportional to the principal curvatures of the DoG surface at that point. An edge point has one large curvature across the edge and one small curvature along it — exactly the Harris "corner vs. edge" signature. Rather than compute eigenvalues, use trace and determinant just like Section 1:

$$\text{Tr}(\mathbf{H}) = D_{xx}+D_{yy} = \lambda_1+\lambda_2 \qquad \text{Det}(\mathbf{H}) = D_{xx}D_{yy}-(D_{xy})^2 = \lambda_1\lambda_2$$

Let \(r=\lambda_1/\lambda_2\) be the ratio of the larger to the smaller curvature. A short bit of algebra shows:

$$\frac{\text{Tr}(\mathbf{H})^2}{\text{Det}(\mathbf{H})} = \frac{(r+1)^2}{r}$$

This quantity is minimized when \(r=1\) (both curvatures equal — a corner-like blob) and grows as \(r\) grows (one curvature dominates — edge-like). So: reject the keypoint if this ratio exceeds the threshold for some maximum acceptable \(r\); Lowe's paper, and this lecture, use \(r=10\):

$$\text{reject if } \frac{\text{Tr}(\mathbf{H})^2}{\text{Det}(\mathbf{H})} > \frac{(r+1)^2}{r} \Big|_{r=10} = 12.1$$

The slides' worked example continues the same running count: 729 → 536 keypoints after this second test.

Both tests, run together on the DoG pyramid built in Section 6:

# outlier_rejection.py
def hessian_2d(D, x, y):
    Dxx = D[y, x+1] - 2*D[y,x] + D[y, x-1]
    Dyy = D[y+1, x] - 2*D[y,x] + D[y-1, x]
    Dxy = (D[y+1,x+1] - D[y+1,x-1] - D[y-1,x+1] + D[y-1,x-1]) / 4.0
    return Dxx, Dyy, Dxy

r_thresh = 10
good_keypoints = []
for x, y, sigma in keypoints:
    Dxx, Dyy, Dxy = hessian_2d(D, x, y)
    Tr, Det = Dxx+Dyy, Dxx*Dyy - Dxy**2
    if Det <= 0:
        continue                                  # curvatures disagree in sign -> not a blob
    if (Tr**2) / Det < (r_thresh+1)**2 / r_thresh:
        good_keypoints.append((x, y, sigma))                 # keep: corner-like, not edge-like

8. Step 3 — Orientation assignment

Every surviving keypoint now has a stable \((x,y,\sigma)\). To make the eventual descriptor rotation-invariant, give each keypoint a canonical orientation up front, so the descriptor can always be measured relative to that orientation rather than relative to the image's fixed x-axis.

8.1 Local gradients

At the keypoint's own scale, compute the gradient magnitude and orientation of the smoothed image \(L\) using simple central differences:

$$m(x,y) = \sqrt{(L(x{+}1,y)-L(x{-}1,y))^2 + (L(x,y{+}1)-L(x,y{-}1))^2}$$ $$\theta(x,y) = \tan^{-1}\!\Big(\frac{L(x,y{+}1)-L(x,y{-}1)}{L(x{+}1,y)-L(x{-}1,y)}\Big)$$

8.2 The weighted histogram

Build a 36-bin histogram of these orientations (one bin per 10°) over a neighborhood around the keypoint, where each pixel's vote is weighted by:

  • its gradient magnitude \(m(x,y)\), and
  • a spatial Gaussian window with \(\sigma = 1.5\times\)(keypoint's own scale) — so pixels closer to the keypoint count more.

The dominant peak of that histogram becomes the keypoint's orientation. If a second peak exists within 80% of the maximum, an additional keypoint is created at the same location and scale but with that second orientation — this is how SIFT handles corners or textures with more than one strong gradient direction, rather than forcing an arbitrary single choice.

Run end to end on a real keypoint location (the badge on the lecture's sample photo's hat — plenty of strong, consistent gradients):

# orientation_assignment.py
L = ndimage.gaussian_filter(img, sigma=keypoint_sigma)
Ly, Lx = np.gradient(L)
mag   = np.sqrt(Lx**2 + Ly**2)
theta = (np.degrees(np.arctan2(Ly, Lx)) + 360) % 360

gauss_weight = np.exp(-((xx-kx)**2 + (yy-ky)**2) / (2*(1.5*keypoint_sigma)**2))
weights = patch_mag * gauss_weight

hist, _ = np.histogram(patch_theta, bins=np.linspace(0,360,37), weights=weights)
dominant_angle = bin_centers[np.argmax(hist)]

9. Step 4 — The 128-D descriptor

9.1 Biological motivation (a brief aside)

The slides draw a deliberate parallel to primate vision: complex cells in visual cortex respond to a gradient at a particular orientation, and tolerate the feature shifting a little within the cell's receptive field (Edelman, Intrator & Poggio, 1997). Pooling many orientation-selective, position-tolerant responses over a neighborhood — which is exactly what's about to happen below — was experimentally shown to give better recognition accuracy under out-of-plane rotation. SIFT's descriptor construction is a direct, engineered version of that idea.

9.2 Construction

  1. Take a 16×16 neighborhood around the keypoint, at the keypoint's scale, and rotate all gradient orientations by −(the keypoint's own orientation from Section 8) — this is precisely what makes the rest of the descriptor rotation-invariant.
  2. Split the 16×16 region into a 4×4 grid of cells (16 cells, each 4×4 pixels).
  3. In each cell, build an 8-bin orientation histogram (45° per bin), with votes weighted by gradient magnitude and a spatial Gaussian centered on the keypoint (same idea as Section 8, applied per cell).
  4. Concatenate all 16 histograms × 8 bins each: \(16 \times 8 = \mathbf{128}\) numbers — the raw descriptor vector.

9.3 Normalization — making it robust to lighting

  1. Normalize to unit length. This buys invariance to uniform (affine) brightness/contrast changes — scaling every pixel's intensity by a constant scales every gradient magnitude by the same constant, which unit-normalization simply divides back out.
  2. Clip large values. Non-linear illumination changes (e.g. camera saturation, specular highlights) can blow up a handful of gradient magnitudes disproportionately. Bound every entry of the unit vector to a maximum of 0.2, which caps the influence of any single dominant gradient.
  3. Renormalize to unit length a second time, since clipping changed the vector's norm.
# descriptor_normalization.py
v = histogram_vector_128d
v = v / np.linalg.norm(v)              # 1. unit length
v = np.clip(v, 0, 0.2)                  # 2. bound large entries
v = v / np.linalg.norm(v)              # 3. renormalize

In practice you'll almost never hand-roll this — OpenCV computes the full, correctly-normalized 128-D descriptor for you:

# real_sift_descriptors.py
import cv2
sift = cv2.SIFT_create()
keypoints, descriptors = sift.detectAndCompute(img, None)
print(descriptors.shape)   # (num_keypoints, 128)

10. Matching keypoints: nearest neighbor + the ratio test

With a 128-D descriptor at every keypoint in both images, correspondence (Section 1's original goal) is finally just a nearest-neighbor search: for each descriptor in image 1, find the descriptor in image 2 with the smallest Euclidean distance.

10.1 Lowe's ratio test

The fix is simple and effective: for each descriptor, find not just the best match but also the second-best match, and look at the ratio of their distances:

$$\text{ratio} = \frac{d(\text{best match})}{d(\text{second-best match})}$$

If the best match is genuinely much better than the second-best, the ratio is small and you can trust the match. If the best and second-best are nearly tied, the match is ambiguous — likely repetitive texture or noise — and should be discarded, no matter how small the absolute distance was.

10.2 Running it for real

Two views of the same photo (one rotated 15°, scaled to 80%, and brightened — simulating a different camera viewpoint and lighting), matched with OpenCV's brute-force matcher and Lowe's ratio test:

# sift_matching.py
import cv2

sift = cv2.SIFT_create()
kp1, des1 = sift.detectAndCompute(img1, None)
kp2, des2 = sift.detectAndCompute(img2, None)

bf = cv2.BFMatcher()
knn_matches = bf.knnMatch(des1, des2, k=2)             # best + second-best, per descriptor

ratio_thresh = 0.75
good_matches = [m for m, n in knn_matches if m.distance < ratio_thresh * n.distance]

match_img = cv2.drawMatches(img1, kp1, img2, kp2, good_matches, None)
Threshold in practice Lowe's paper recommends 0.8 as a good general-purpose threshold; many practical pipelines tighten it to 0.7–0.75 (as used above) when they'd rather have fewer, more confident matches — e.g. for geometric verification (RANSAC + homography) where a handful of clean matches beats a pile of noisy ones.

11. Cheat sheet & full reference script

StageKey formula / ruleTypical constant
Harris (recap)\(har=\det\mu-\alpha(\text{trace}\,\mu)^2\)\(\alpha\approx0.04\–0.06\)
LoG\(\nabla^2L=L_{xx}+L_{yy}\), peak across scalepeak near \(\sigma=r/\sqrt2\)
DoG ≈ LoG\(G(k\sigma)-G(\sigma)\approx(k{-}1)\sigma^2\nabla^2G\)—
Pyramidoctave doubles \(\sigma\); \(k=2^{1/s}\) within octave\(s=3,\ \sigma_0=1.6\)
Extrema testcompare to 26 neighbours (space + scale)—
Low-contrast reject\(|D(\hat{\mathbf{x}})| < \) threshold0.03
Edge reject\(\text{Tr}(H)^2/\text{Det}(H) > (r{+}1)^2/r\)\(r=10\)

Matchingratio = best / second-best distancethreshold ≈ 0.8

Everything above, consolidated into one runnable file:

"""
sift_full_pipeline.py
Run: python sift_full_pipeline.py
Requires: numpy, scipy, opencv-python, pillow
"""
import numpy as np
from scipy import ndimage
import cv2
from PIL import Image

# ---------- 1. build a DoG scale-space pyramid (one octave shown) ----------
img = np.array(Image.open("photo.jpg").convert("L"), dtype=float) / 255.0
sigma0, k, n_scales = 1.6, 2**(1.0/3), 6
gaussians = [ndimage.gaussian_filter(img, sigma=sigma0*(k**i)) for i in range(n_scales)]
dogs      = [gaussians[i+1] - gaussians[i] for i in range(n_scales-1)]
stack     = np.stack(dogs, axis=0)

# ---------- 2. scale-space extrema (26-neighbour test) ----------
contrast_thresh, candidates = 0.03, []
for s in range(1, stack.shape[0]-1):
    cur, prev, nxt = stack[s], stack[s-1], stack[s+1]
    nmax = np.maximum.reduce([ndimage.maximum_filter(im,3) for im in (cur,prev,nxt)])
    nmin = np.minimum.reduce([ndimage.minimum_filter(im,3) for im in (cur,prev,nxt)])
    keep = ((cur>=nmax)|(cur<=nmin)) & (np.abs(cur)>contrast_thresh)
    for y,x in np.argwhere(keep):
        candidates.append((x,y,s))

# ---------- 3. edge-response rejection (Tr^2/Det ratio test) ----------
def hessian_2d(D,x,y):
    Dxx = D[y,x+1]-2*D[y,x]+D[y,x-1]
    Dyy = D[y+1,x]-2*D[y,x]+D[y-1,x]
    Dxy = (D[y+1,x+1]-D[y+1,x-1]-D[y-1,x+1]+D[y-1,x-1])/4.0
    return Dxx,Dyy,Dxy

r_thresh, good = 10, []
for x,y,s in candidates:
    Dxx,Dyy,Dxy = hessian_2d(stack[s],x,y)
    Tr,Det = Dxx+Dyy, Dxx*Dyy-Dxy**2
    if Det>0 and (Tr**2)/Det < (r_thresh+1)**2/r_thresh:
        good.append((x,y,s))

print(f"{len(candidates)} raw extrema -> {len(good)} after edge rejection")

# ---------- 4-6. orientation + descriptor + matching: use OpenCV directly ----------
img1 = cv2.imread("photo1.jpg", cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
img2 = cv2.imread("photo2.jpg", cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)

sift = cv2.SIFT_create()
kp1, des1 = sift.detectAndCompute(img1, None)
kp2, des2 = sift.detectAndCompute(img2, None)

bf = cv2.BFMatcher()
knn_matches = bf.knnMatch(des1, des2, k=2)
good_matches = [m for m,n in knn_matches if m.distance < 0.75*n.distance]
print(f"{len(good_matches)} good matches out of {len(knn_matches)} keypoints")

match_img = cv2.drawMatches(img1, kp1, img2, kp2, good_matches[:40], None)
cv2.imwrite("matches.png", match_img)

12. Exam recap — the 12 things to remember

  1. Harris corners localize in \(x\)-\(y\) but use a fixed window — they're not scale-invariant. SIFT exists to fix exactly that gap.
  2. Scale space (Witkin) means examining a signal at a whole spectrum of blur levels and trusting whatever survives across scales (spatial coincidence assumption).
  3. LoG = \(L_{xx}+L_{yy}\); its scale-normalized response to a blob of radius \(r\) peaks near \(\sigma=r/\sqrt2\) — this is the basis of all scale selection in SIFT.
  4. DoG approximates LoG: \(G(k\sigma)-G(\sigma)\approx(k{-}1)\sigma^2\nabla^2G\), derived from the heat equation \(\partial G/\partial\sigma=\sigma\nabla^2G\). Cheap to compute — just subtract pyramid levels.
  5. The pyramid is organized into octaves; within an octave \(\sigma\) grows by \(k=2^{1/s}\) each step; crossing into the next octave doubles \(\sigma\) and halves image resolution.
  6. Standard constants (empirically justified by repeatability experiments): \(s=3\) scales/octave, base \(\sigma_0=1.6\).
  7. Extrema detection: compare each DoG pixel to all 26 neighbours across space and scale.
  8. Localization: Taylor-expand \(D\), solve \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}=-H^{-1}\nabla D\) for the sub-pixel offset; reject if \(|D(\hat{\mathbf{x}})|<0.03\) (low contrast).
  9. Edge rejection: reject if \(\text{Tr}(H)^2/\text{Det}(H) > (r{+}1)^2/r\) at \(r=10\) — same determinant/trace trick as Harris, applied to the DoG's own Hessian.
  10. Orientation: 36-bin gradient histogram weighted by magnitude × Gaussian(\(1.5\sigma\)); dominant peak sets the keypoint's orientation; secondary peaks >80% of max spawn extra keypoints.
  11. Descriptor: 16×16 neighbourhood → 4×4 cells × 8-bin histograms = 128-D vector; unit-normalize, clip at 0.2, renormalize.
  12. Matching: nearest neighbor by Euclidean distance, filtered by Lowe's ratio test (best/second-best < ≈0.8) to reject ambiguous matches from repetitive structure.
